lesson.title: The Niche: An Organism's Address and Occupation
lesson.summary: An organism's ecological niche is the full set of environmental conditions and resources it needs to survive and reproduce, and ecologists distinguish between the niche a species could theoretically occupy and the narrower niche it actually occupies once competition and other pressures are factored in.
lesson.body:
A useful shorthand that some ecologists use is that a species' habitat is its address, the physical place where it lives, while its niche is its occupation, the full role it plays there. More formally, an organism's ecological niche includes everything it needs to survive and reproduce: the temperature range it can tolerate, the food it eats, the space it requires, the time of day or year it is active, and how it interacts with every other species around it. This idea builds on the levels of ecological organization you have already encountered, since a niche is really a description of how one species fits into its population, its community, and its ecosystem all at once.

Ecologists often separate two versions of the niche concept, an idea developed in detail by the ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson in the late 1950s. The fundamental niche is the full range of conditions and resources a species could theoretically use if nothing else got in its way, no competitors, no predators, no other constraints. The realized niche is the narrower set of conditions and resources a species actually uses in the real world, once competition and other pressures are taken into account. The gap between these two versions of the niche is often where competition leaves its clearest fingerprint.

The barnacle experiment described earlier, in the chapter on competition, is also one of the best illustrations of the difference between a fundamental and a realized niche. Recall that Chthamalus stellatus could survive and grow across a wide vertical range of the shore, including lower zones, when its competitor Semibalanus balanoides was experimentally removed. That wide range was its fundamental niche. But under normal conditions, with Semibalanus present and outcompeting it lower down, Chthamalus was squeezed into only the upper, drier part of the shore. That narrower range was its realized niche. The same logic applies to resource partitioning: when species divide up space, timing, or food type to reduce competition, each species' realized niche typically ends up narrower and more specialized than its fundamental niche would allow.

Thinking in terms of niches gives ecologists a powerful, unifying way to connect ideas that might otherwise seem separate. Competition happens when two species' niches overlap too much for both to thrive. Resource partitioning is essentially a shift in realized niches that reduces that overlap. And the competitive exclusion principle can be restated in niche language: no two species can occupy the identical realized niche indefinitely in the same place. Keeping the niche concept in mind as you move forward will make it easier to see how the different community interactions in this unit, competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism, all describe different kinds of relationships between species' niches.
